advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Make the 'immediately-previous release' selection deterministic even when two builds share a second-granularity CreatedAt (e.g. tie-break on an explicit build ordinal / creation nanoseconds, not the random sha).
evidence: infra/scripts/autodeploy.sh:528:            { print r; exit }                           # newest remaining = immediately-previous

Comment claims 'pick the immediately-previous release deterministically' (line 492) but docker CreatedAt is second-granularity; same-second builds tie and sort -r falls back to lexical order of the random sha, so 'newest remaining' is not reliably the true previous release.
infra/scripts/autodeploy.sh:526:     tag !~ /^[0-9a-f]{40}$/ { next }            # only per-release <sha> tags
infra/scripts/autodeploy.sh:533:     case "$tag" in *[!0-9a-f]*|"") continue ;; esac   # only per-release <sha> tags (guard 1)

The shell loop deliberately avoids interval regexes and uses a portable case-glob + length test for the identical 40-hex-sha check; the awk uses {40}, an interval expression that some awk builds ignore/treat literally, diverging behavior between the two guards.
advisory.finding: The 'immediately-previous release' preserved for rollback is chosen by lexically sorting docker's CreatedAt, which has only second granularity; when two releases share a build timestamp the tie is broken by the (effectively random) 40-hex sha, so prev_ref is non-deterministic and reconcile can retire the image a rollback actually depends on while keeping an older one.
merged_from: prev_ref uses an awk interval-expression regex /^[0-9a-f]{40}$/ while the parallel guard in the shell loop uses portable char-class + length tests; awk interval expressions are not universally enabled by default (old mawk/gawk without --re-interval), so on such an interpreter prev_ref could match nothing and the true previous release would be treated as a removable orphan.
scenarios: Two mcp releases built within the same wall-clock second; reconcile keeps whichever sha sorts higher and may retire the genuinely-newer previous release, leaving a stale image as the only rollback target.

blocking.checklist_item: - [ ] Anchor the fail-safe test with a presence assertion that the reconcile stage reached the live-unknown branch (e.g. assert the 'live image unknown; skipping orphan sweep (fail-safe)' log line appears in result.stdout) before trusting the empty-removals absence check.
evidence: Test assertion: `assert _image_removals(cmds) == [], ("with the live image unidentifiable, reconcile must fail SAFE and remove nothing...")`
Only liveness anchor is `assert result.returncode == 0` — proves the tick completed, not that the reconcile stage executed the fail-safe branch
Source emits a distinctive fail-safe log the test could assert PRESENCE of: autodeploy.sh:519 `log "mcp reconcile: live image unknown; skipping orphan sweep (fail-safe)"`
`log()` (autodeploy.sh:272) printf's to stdout, which the test captures in `result.stdout` but never asserts on
Unlike the other three new tests, this one uses a bare `time.sleep(1.0)` + `_commands()` with no `_commands_eventually` needle establishing that any reconcile-stage activity occurred
blocking.finding: The fail-safe test asserts only the ABSENCE of image removals (`_image_removals(cmds) == []`) from the subprocess call log with no anchor that the orphan-reconcile stage was actually reached; it passes both when the fail-safe branch correctly fired AND in any world where mcp_reconcile_orphans never ran, so it cannot distinguish a working fail-safe from a reconcile path that was silently skipped.
scenarios: A future refactor that fails to call mcp_reconcile_orphans from mcp_retire_sweep on this tick would leave this test green — it would not detect the regression that the fail-safe path stopped being exercised
blocking.suggested_fix: Add `assert "skipping orphan sweep (fail-safe)" in result.stdout, ctx` before the `_image_removals(cmds) == []` assertion, so the test proves the reconcile fail-safe branch actually executed rather than passing when reconcile never ran.
